"I’m disappointed that we didn’t listen with ears, okay, I hear you, I understand. Let’s figure out how we can do what you want, but also what we believe would be in the best interest of the community."

articles.title: SCOTUS slams door on Dem judge’s career fight after years of pro-Biden Facebook posts
articles.summary: The Supreme Court declined to hear Mark Cohen's First Amendment appeal after the Pennsylvania judge was suspended over dozens of political Facebook posts.
articles.body: The Supreme Court declined Monday to hear an appeal from a former Pennsylvania judge who was suspended after repeatedly posting partisan political content on Facebook, including praise for former President Joe Biden and his policies. Former Judge Mark Cohen, a former Democratic state lawmaker who began serving on the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas in 2018, made dozens of politically charged Facebook posts while on the bench, even after being warned to stop. Cohen appealed to the Supreme Court in April, with his lawyers arguing that the former judge’s First Amendment rights had been violated. "Allowing judges to be disciplined based on the perceived ‘tone’ or ‘volume’ of lawful speech promotes arbitrary enforcement, invites political interference in the judicial branch, and threatens to undermine the rule of law," Cohen’s lawyer told Law.com at the time. "This case presents an urgent opportunity for the court to restore constitutional clarity and reestablish the First Amendment’s protection of the rights of sitting judges to speak on matters of public concern." DOJ MOVES TO BOOT FEDERAL JUDGES FROM IMMIGRATION CASES OVER NYT INTERVIEW The Supreme Court declined to take up Cohen’s case, denying his petition without comment. Pennsylvania’s Judicial Conduct Board argued that the Supreme Court did not need to hear Cohen’s appeal because his social media activity amounted to "partisan cheerleading" and his suspension reflected a "straightforward application of familiar rules that judges around the country have followed for decades." FETTERMAN WEIGHS IN AFTER PA SUPREME COURT JUSTICE APPARENTLY SPLITS FROM DEMOCRATIC PARTY OVER ANTISEMITISM Pennsylvania’s highest court concluded that the volume and tone of Cohen’s posts made him appear to be an advocate for the Democratic Party. In November 2021, Cohen promoted Biden’s Build Back Better legislation, saying its passage would improve "many, many American lives." A year later, on Biden’s birthday, Cohen called him "an excellent President" and said he looked forward to "many more achievements." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS Cohen also made posts taking specific policy positions, including one in favor of higher minimum wage laws and another against restrictions on elective abortions. Cohen also highlighted his record on gun policy, including a post noting that he had consistently received an "F" rating from the National Rifle Association while serving in the state legislature. Cohen’s Supreme Court petition says the suspension also triggered the forfeiture of his judicial and prior public-service pensions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP DLA Piper, the law firm representing Cohen, did not respond Wednesday to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

articles.title: Trump reveals surprise American taxpayer stake in new $6.6B submarine deal
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced a 40% taxpayer stake in Anduril's Arsenal-2 shipyard subsidiary, adding government ownership to the $6.6 billion deal.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced the U.S. government will take a 40% stake in the new shipyard being built in Baltimore to boost submarine production, adding a major government ownership component to the $6.6 billion project. "The ultimate proof of our commitment to ensuring the shipyard's enduring success: American taxpayers will receive a 40 percent stake in the new shipyard," Trump said during remarks in Sparrows Point on Tuesday. "We get 40 percent." Anduril has said the stake will be in a new subsidiary created to operate the Arsenal-2 shipyard, rather than in the defense tech company itself. Further details about what rights come with the government's 40% interest, what the government is providing in exchange and how it could ultimately generate a return have not yet been publicly released. Fox News Digital has reached out to Anduril and the White House for details. STARTUPS BRING INNOVATION TO DEFENSE INDUSTRIAL BASE The size of the stake stands out even as the Trump administration has increasingly taken direct government interests in companies and projects it considers critical to national security. The administration has struck equity arrangements involving chipmaker Intel, rare earths producer MP Materials and other strategic industries. The arrangement is part of a broader $6.6 billion effort to expand production of Virginia-class attack submarines as the U.S. struggles to keep pace with China's vast shipbuilding capacities and the Navy falls behind on its production goal. Anduril is committing $3.7 billion of its own capital to build the facility and manufacturing capacity, while the Navy could spend up to $2.9 billion purchasing what it produces. The project is aimed at closing a persistent U.S. submarine production shortfall as China rapidly expands its naval and shipbuilding capacity. American shipyards are delivering roughly 1.3 Virginia-class attack submarines a year, short of the Navy's goal of two, which it does not expect to reach until around 2032. Once fully operational, Arsenal-2 is expected to add about 9 million labor hours annually to the submarine industrial base, increasing Virginia-class production capacity by roughly 15%, an administration official told reporters on a call before Trump’s remarks. LARGEST-EVER US STEEL PLANT IS COMING TO A KEY RED STATE AS TRUMP UNVEILS $15B INVESTMENT An industry official on the call emphasized that Anduril would finance the new production capacity itself while the government paid for the resulting output. "I wouldn't say that the government's paying us back. We feel the government [is] buying the results of what we're able to produce," the industry official said. The 40% government stake was not disclosed on the call, which included questions from reporters about how the project would be financed. The submarine crunch is part of a broader shipbuilding gap with China, whose vast commercial maritime industry also supports its rapidly expanding navy. China now accounts for more than half of global commercial shipbuilding output, while the U.S. accounts for only a fraction of 1%, giving Beijing an enormous industrial base that can also support military ship construction. Anduril plans to begin with critical components including torpedo tubes, which a senior administration official described as a current "gating component" slowing Virginia-class production. The company eventually plans to manufacture larger modules and sections of submarines at Arsenal-2. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The more than 2 million-square-foot facility is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and roughly 11,000 indirect jobs nationwide, with operations slated to begin around 2030.

articles.title: Biden's 'weaponized' Mar-a-Lago raid slammed by White House as declassified docs reveal FBI's legal doubts
articles.summary: Declassified emails reveal the FBI's Washington Field Office told the DOJ it lacked probable cause for the Mar-a-Lago raid weeks before it happened.
articles.body: The White House ripped Joe Biden after documents declassified by President Donald Trump on Monday revealed internal strife between the former president's Department of Justice (DOJ) and the FBI's Washington Field Office (WFO) before carrying out a raid on Mar-a-Lago in 2022. In the months leading up to the raid, internal emails between FBI agents in the field office expressed frustration that the DOJ, led by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland, was unresponsive to their requests and unwilling to consider alternative options to raiding Trump's estate in Palm Beach, Florida a year-and-a-half after he left office after his first term. Fox News Digital exclusively reported on the internal emails, which show the FBI didn't believe it had probable cause to execute the warrant, in December. "Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple," the White House said Tuesday. "This is further proof the Biden administration weaponized the DOJ to target political opponents. Those responsible must be held accountable." TODD BLANCHE REVEALS DOJ UNEARTHED CACHE OF JACK SMITH DOCUMENTS INSIDE FORGOTTEN ROOM An email dated May 24, 2022, with the subject line "PE (Plasma Echo) Next steps - timeline preference - UNCLASSIFIED," the special agent in charge of the counterintelligence division of the WFO sent an internal email detailing a proposed timeline for the investigation, ending with the execution of a search warrant. That target date was June 6 of that year. The raid would eventually take place on Aug. 8, 2022. Another agent replied asking the first to loop the DOJ in on the timeline. What followed was skepticism that the raid was even necessary. "[REDACTED] and I also agreed if there was a way to obtain the records via the [REDACTED], without the execution of the SW (search warrant), it would be preferable," the special agent in charge said. Another batch of internal emails from June 1-2, 2022, shows the FBI seeking a potential off-ramp from the investigation that was heading towards the execution of the raid. "Even as we continue down the path towards a search warrant, WFO believes that a reasonable conversation with the former President's attorney, [REDACTED], ought not to be discounted," the email said. "At a minimum, even if the former President's attorney is correct and that the documents were all declassified (or believed to be declassified), it can be reasonably argued that the documents remain sensitive and should be properly secured until the matter of classification is sorted out. This conversation could easily be accomplished at the same time that WFO presses forward with the investigation and continues building out the search warrant." JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS The emails noted that Trump's defense attorneys would likely argue that the president has the absolute authority to declassify documents and expressed frustration that the DOJ, despite being asked, had not provided the FBI with a list of the charges they might file. An internal email from July 13, 2022, less than a month before the raid, the assistant special agent in charge of the WFO said flatly that the FBI didn't believe there was probable cause for the raid. "WFO does not believe (and has articulated to DOJ CES), that we have established probable cause for the search warrant at Mar a Lago. DOJ has opined that they do, requesting the a wide scope including residence, office, storage space," that email says. The agent annoyedly continued by implying that the DOJ wasn't interested in recovering the allegedly mishandled classified documents, intimating that there may have been an ulterior motive. "Finally, if the goal is to identify and recover classified records quickly, so as to protect the information, the 5 weeks spent fixated on probable cause for a search warrant have been counterproductive," the email said. The agent offered other solutions to the raid, including re-interviewing Trump's attorney and attempting to find other material witnesses. BIDEN-ERA FBI TRACKED TRUMP FAMILY TRAVEL AND WILES' CALLS WITH LAWYERS IN SECRET PROBE: DOCS "A reasonable step would be to recontact the attorney and inquire about any further documents. WFO has made numerous suggestions to DOJ over the course of this investigation that the most expedient way to ensure recovery of all classified documents would be to go through [REDACTED]. DOJ has persistently disagreed. Other documents declassified by the White House Monday showed that the FBI tapped now-White House chief of staff Susie Wiles' phone and tracked the movements of Melania and Barron Trump. The raid on Trump's Florida estate was viewed as politically driven by many, as Trump was at the time mulling what became a successful bid for the presidency in 2024. DOJ-appointed special counsel Jack Smith investigated the alleged retention of classified materials. Trump pleaded not guilty to all 37 felony charges from Smith’s probe, including willful retention of national defense information, conspiracy to obstruct justice and false statements. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A superseding indictment charged Trump with three more alleged crimes: another count of willful retention of national defense information and two additional obstruction counts. Trump pleaded not guilty, and Smith dropped after Trump won the 2024 presidential election.

articles.title: Trump wants to turn his West Palm Beach golf club into the new Camp David
articles.summary: Much of President Donald Trump’s second term has focused on changes to the nation’s capital. But his ambitions to remake the physical architecture of the pre...
articles.body:
Much of President Donald Trump's second term has focused on changes to the nation's capital.

But his ambitions to remake the physical architecture of the presidency transcend Washington: Trump wants to transform his West Palm Beach golf club into a presidential retreat modeled after Camp David.

The plan calls for a parcel of the private club to be designated a permanent, official sanctuary for foreign leaders and future U.S. presidents, designed to host international summits and house presidents when they take vacations in Florida, according to a proposal presented to Palm Beach County officials by Trump International Golf Club's legal counsel. Future presidents would also be offered comped memberships to the Trump club.

"Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County," Harvey Oyer, a lawyer representing the Trump course, wrote to the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners in a letter last month. Oyer asked the county, which owns the property the course is on, to provide a piece of the land to the federal government, and he promised Trump would pay for the construction of a presidential residence and facilities on that land.

Oyer told The Washington Post that a name has yet not been selected for the presidential golf course.

"It would further cement Palm Beach County as one of the most recognizable brands and destinations in the world," Oyer said.

A spokesperson for the Trump Organization did not respond to requests for comment.

A White House official with knowledge of the proposed plans said in a text message the facilities would provide amenities of a "world-class property."

"The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly rated golf course. These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat," said the White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preview plans.

In the letter, which was first reported by the Palm Beach Post, Oyer said the construction would not be completed before Trump leaves office, so the project would be "a gift" to Trump's successors and the county would benefit from high-power traffic in the area.

The county is seriously considering the proposal and is seeking more information, Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo told The Washington Post. In a meeting last week, Trump representatives assured county officials that, under the proposal, Trump's company would continue to make lease payments for the golf course and would agree to build the presidential retreat on a connected piece of land that would have a separate entrance from the private club, Abruzzo said.

Trump's club would continue to operate under the Trump family company and would probably benefit from more business if it becomes a site of long-lasting presidential importance.

The county is in contact with the General Services Administration, the agency that manages federal properties, and the county will be selecting a parcel of the land for the proposal, Abruzzo said.

"My understanding is that President Trump views this as a lasting contribution to the presidency and to those who will hold the office after him," Abruzzo said.

Though presidents already have a retreat at Camp David, Trump has visited the complex less frequently than many of his predecessors, preferring to spend his weekends and holidays at his own properties. He once commented that Camp David's rustic charm would wear off after half an hour.

Previous presidents have left their own marks on the woodsy Maryland retreat. Franklin D. Roosevelt established the getaway for federal workers as a presidential compound and dubbed it Shangri-La, though Dwight D. Eisenhower later named it after his father and grandson.

Marjorie Merriweather Post, who was once the wealthiest woman in the United States, also had hoped to create a presidential retreat in the South. She gifted her Palm Beach estate - better known as Mar-a-Lago - to the federal government upon her death in 1973, with the intention that it be turned into a Winter White House. But the National Park Service returned the property to her estate due to high maintenance costs, and Trump bought the property in 1985.

Trump International Golf Club opened in 1999 after Trump settled a lawsuit with the county regarding airplanes flying over Mar-a-Lago and the county agreed to lend him the land. Near the golf course, state officials have branded the Palm Beach airport and the road along it with Trump's name.

Trump's influence over Palm Beach and its image would be further cemented if the golf club becomes a presidential retreat. The wealthy strip of South Florida has undergone a MAGA transformation with Trump's base flocking to Mar-a-Lago for political events and networking. The nearby golf club has become a go-to destination for Trump spotting.

Trump reported an income of nearly $37 million last year from the golf course in his latest financial disclosure.

Although Trump had mocked former president Barack Obama for golfing during his presidency, Trump has frequently golfed since he has been in office. One online tracker calculated that Trump has spent at least 137 days in his second term golfing.

Rick Reilly, a former Sports Illustrated columnist who wrote "Commander in Cheat: How Golf Explains Trump," has golfed with Trump and said the president is less interested in the sport than the attention he gains at his own clubs. Reilly described how Trump always plays first in his golfing party and speeds on his golf cart to the next hole, wrapping up his game in less time than is typical, before heading to the clubhouse, where he makes the rounds, talking to his members and fans. If the Palm Beach club were a destination for foreign leaders, they would be part of the display of influence.

"I suppose he wants to make a power play with these people and show them who is the king of America," Reilly said.

Don Van Natta Jr., an ESPN senior writer who wrote "First Off the Tee: Presidential Hackers, Duffers, and Cheaters From Taft to Bush," a book on the history of presidents who golfed, said 17 of the past 20 presidents have golfed. The first avid golfer in the Oval Office was William Howard Taft, and the last president who didn't golf was Jimmy Carter.

"There is a long history of presidents playing golf," Van Natta said. "It's an escape where they can, as President [Bill] Clinton told me for my book, to be out in nature, and it's an escape hatch from the pressures of the Oval Office."

articles.title: Trump sons' investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election
articles.summary: The contract for a new plant in Baltimore is the latest linked to the brothers.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced a $6.6 billion investment with AI defense company Anduril Industries on Tuesday -- the most recent government funding agreement into a company with investment ties to the president's sons.

The Trump administration announced the Navy will support $2.9 billion of the total cost to help create a new facility in Baltimore County, Maryland, that will manufacture critical parts for the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine.

"In a tremendous victory for our country and for the city of Baltimore, Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in a state-of-the-art shipyard that will be known forever as Arsenal-2," Trump said at an event announcing the investment.

"Right here in Sparrows Point, you'll build the next generation of American submarines, including autonomous subs, torpedo tubes, and critical components for our cutting edge Virginia-class attack submarines," Trump said.

1789 Capital -- a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders -- claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.

Since that investment, Anduril has been awarded 135 other contracts with the U.S. government and to date has received around $1.8 billion from those agreements, according to active defense contracts posted to SAM.gov , the official system for government contracting.

Anduril did not respond for comment on its contracts or investments from 1789 Capital, though the company has been awarded contracts dating back to 2019, according to USASpending.gov

The company is one of the largest manufacturers to receive an investment from Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump, but they are not the only one.

An ABC News analysis found defense companies backed by the president's sons, including Anduril, have now raked in more than $6 billion dollars in active or promised government contracts since those investments were made, according to the government's official contract reporting.

This comes as Congressional Oversight Democrats continue to demand the Pentagon's inspector general investigate the approved deals.

"Refusal to investigate these serious allegations will raise significant concerns about whether your office is able to perform its statutory duty as an independent watchdog over DoD," lawmakers Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren, Robert Garcia and Tammy Duckworth wrote in a letter to Platte B. Moring, III, the Pentagon's inspector general, in May.

A Pentagon official told ABC News, "No company receives preferential treatment. The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity. Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department's funding decisions."

A spokesperson for the Trump brothers denied any wrongdoing.

"Don and Eric are experienced business leaders who have built and invested in businesses across a wide range of industries for decades, long before their father first ran for public office. Their investment decisions are based solely on their independent business judgment and personal convictions and they do not seek to influence, direct, or participate in any government decision, procurement, award, regulatory action, or other governmental process. Attempts to portray their ordinary investment activities as improper are a deliberate distortion of the facts," the spokesperson said.

Shortly after Trump won the presidency, Donald Trump Jr. was named an adviser for Florida-based drone manufacturer Unusual Machines -- a company which had not previously won any government contracts.

In October 2025, Unusual Machines scored a direct U.S. Dept. of Defense agreement for 3,500 orders of National Defense Authorization Act-compliant motors, with a potential order of 20,000 on the way in 2026.

The Trump brothers are also listed as "notable investors" for the U.S. drone company Powerus, the company announced in March 2026.

Despite not having any government contracts previously, Powerus won its first Air Force purchase order just one month later for an undisclosed amount.

In July, Powerus was awarded up to $90 million for aerial-denial unmanned aircraft systems from the U.S. Air Force.

ABC News asked Powerus if it was concerned at all about the involvement of the Trump brothers in the company, given its active contracts.

"Defense procurement is merit-based. You can't sell the government something that won't protect a soldier, and nobody in the procurement chain risks their career routing a contract to a company whose equipment doesn't work," a spokesperson for Powerus said.

"Neither Donald Trump Jr. nor Eric Trump is an advisor to Powerus, and neither is involved in the company's day-to-day business," the spokesperson continued. "Their interest is indirect, held through American Ventures, an investor in the company."

Trump-linked investments extend into the manufacturing industry, with the brothers combining for more than $1 billion across companies in mining, quantum computing and aerospace.

Oversight Democrats in their letter to the DoD criticized Donald Trump Jr.'s portfolio in raw materials, citing an August 2025 investment into Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth mining company harvesting critical materials for defense manufacturing.

That same month, the Office of Strategic Capital loaned Vulcan Elements $620 million to expand its operation.

Vulcan Elements did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts and the investments from 1789 Capital.

The firm also invested $60 million in Texas-based Firehawk Aerospace, according to firm portfolios provided by PitchBook. In the same month, Firehawk won a $4.9 million Air Force contract to "Advance Hybrid Rocket Engine Development," according to a company press release.

Firehawk would later secure tens of millions more -- $3.2 million in May 2026 , an undisclosed "multimillion-dollar" contract with the Air Force Research Laboratory in July and $24 million in Dept. of Defense munitions contracts in August, according to company press releases and active contracts.

Firehawk Aerospace has been awarded government contracts across both the Biden and Trump administrations since the company's founding in 2019.

In a statement to ABC News, Firehawk said its award is "solely the product of engineering expertise and capacity."

"We value the many investors who back that mission and share our conviction that the Nation's arsenal must be built to last. Our focus is the duty in front of us, making the arsenal of the U.S. and our allies stronger," a Firehawk spokesperson said.

ABC News also found 1789 Capital raised $1 billion in revenue generation for California-based PsiQuantum in September of last year, with the company's pre-existing contract with DoD expanding by more than $157 million since then, according to SAM.gov .

PsiQuantum also signed a $100 million letter of intent with the Department of Commerce and another $125 million with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency in May and July of 2026.

PsiQuantum did not respond when asked for comment on these investments.

Trump-linked investments were found in the automation sector.

Eric Trump said he was named chief strategy adviser for Foundation Future Industries, a humanoid robot startup with the stated aim to develop autonomous soldiers and workers.

Eric Trump touted a $24 million contract in April -- the company's first -- according to Eric Trump and CEO Sankaet Pathal's statements on Fox News. Pathal did not respond for comment on this contract or on Trump's involvement with the company's operations.

ABC News found a $391 million 1789 Capital investment into Hadrian -- a highly automated, AI-driven manufacturing company -- in the early days of 2026.

The company won its first public contracts a few months later in March -- a $39.2 million agreement with the Army for machinery and manufacturing and a $900 million deal with the Navy to create highly automated submarine factories.

Hadrian did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts.

Congressional Democrats continue to sound the alarm over these investments, referring ABC News to their May demand to the Department of Defense to launch an investigation into the president's family.

"We hope that your office will take seriously these latest concerns about corruption in the DoD award process and fulfill your statutory responsibility by initiating a review," the lawmakers wrote in their letter.

articles.title: Trump says he’ll terminate LaCivita, Blair if they have consulting conflicts
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday said he would terminate outside consultants Chris LaCivita and James Blair if their work conflicted with the White House, following a report that the two were in the Balkans advising a pro-Russian political party and made hundreds of thousands of dollars. Trump appeared to distance himself from the work LaCivita and…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday said he would terminate outside consultants Chris LaCivita and James Blair if their work conflicted with the White House, following a report that the two were in the Balkans advising a pro-Russian political party and made hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Trump appeared to distance himself from the work LaCivita and Blair did for Republika Srpska, saying that it was fine for his consultants to have additional contracts but that he knew nothing about that work.

“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” he continued. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

The New York Times reported Tuesday that the two went to Republika Srpska, a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The country’s elections are set to be on Sunday.

Blair and LaCivita were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each through a Washington-based law firm that the Republika Srpska’s government hired to provide counsel on voting issues, the outlet reported.

While the Times noted Blair and LaCivita were paid by the government and not the political party behind the government, it wrote that for all intents and purposes work for the government and the party are the same thing.

The work was also notable in that it comes as Republicans are facing an uphill climb to save their House and Senate majorities. Trump has been traveling the U.S. to rally Republican support ahead of the midterms.

Blair served as White House deputy chief of staff but left for a temporary leave of absence in April to run Trump’s political operation for the midterms.

LaCivita previously served as a senior adviser to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

articles.title: DHS unloads on teachers union boss over 'dangerous rhetoric' and anti-ICE activism
articles.summary: Randi Weingarten filmed a video near Newark's Delaney Hall migrant detention facility, drawing sharp criticism from DHS and school choice advocates.
articles.body: American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten drew backlash Wednesday after filming a video from a field near Newark’s Delaney Hall migrant detention facility, where she decried alleged conditions inside. Weingarten’s video, filmed within view of the facility, comes as school-choice advocates have criticized her political activism while student academic performance remains below pre-pandemic levels — with one critic recently summing up the contrast as a desire to "dictate … policy on immigration while its own members’ students struggle with basic skills." "Dangerous rhetoric from politicians and activists demonizing our brave ICE officers has led to the over 8,000% increase in threats against DHS law enforcement who are heroically performing their congressionally mandated mission to remove criminal illegal aliens from communities across the country," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital when asked about Weingarten’s visit. "Any claim that there are subprime conditions at ICE detention facilities is false," the agency said. ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS CLASH WITH AGENTS OUTSIDE NEW JERSEY DETENTION CENTER AS GOV SHERRILL DENIED ENTRY Fox News Digital reached out to Weingarten through AFT for comment. In her video, Weingarten disputed DHS’ characterization of conditions at the facility: "This is one of the most despicable things that our current government does," Weingarten said as she was filmed pointing and gesticulating toward Delaney Hall. "They put people — people have not committed any crimes — they are immigrants. They deport them, or they … detain them and deport them in conditions that are unimaginable." Weingarten, who grew up about 40 miles north of New York City in Nyack, New York, said her grandparents came to the U.S. seeking a better life, drawing a comparison to migrants detained at Delaney Hall. "We saw families coming out [of Delaney] who had just visited their loved ones… They work hard. They play by the rules. They should not be detained or deported because we have a broken immigration system," she claimed. "We should fix the immigration system, but the cruelty of this government right now is terrible." DHS said in response to Weingarten that its mission remains "straightforward" — enforcing laws on the books and protecting America’s national security. "Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now," the DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital. INSPECTION OF DELANEY HALL ICE FACILITY CONTRADICTS CLAIMS IN NEW JERSEY ATTORNEY GENERAL'S LAWSUIT School-choice advocate Corey DeAngelis responded to Weingarten’s video by arguing that the union leader wants more illegal immigrants enrolled in public schools because their enrollment increases taxpayer funding. "It's time to overturn Plyler v Doe and stop forcing taxpayers to fund education for illegals," DeAngelis tweeted, referencing a 1982 Supreme Court case wherein Eisenhower-appointed Justice William Brennan Jr. ruled for the majority that Texas could not deny undocumented school-age children access to free public education. A 2026 Annie E. Casey Foundation analysis found that 47 states fared worse on its education index in 2024 than in 2019, with national declines in math proficiency, reading proficiency and preschool attendance. Weingarten has led AFT since 2008. She previously led New York City’s UFT from 1998 to 2009. DeAngelis previously criticized Weingarten after she encouraged a boycott of Target over the Minnesota-based retailer’s response to ICE operations. DeAngelis wrote for the Heritage Foundation that AFT "wants to dictate corporate policy on immigration while its own members’ students struggle with basic skills. That mismatch should alarm every taxpayer and parent." WATCH: WEINGARTEN GESTURES WILDLY DURING ANTI-TRUMP RANT, LATER SAYS HE DRIVES HER TO DRINK The clip of Weingarten drew criticism on X, including from users who argued that the teachers union leader was straying beyond education policy and into the immigration debate. Other critics shared photos of Weingarten promoting her book "Why Fascists Fear Teachers." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "This is wild. Randi Weingarten is bad enough in her education related field (power, indoctrination, control) but now she is expanding into immigration," another wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The clash comes as Weingarten and AFT have become increasingly involved in immigration fights beyond the classroom, including pressuring Target over ICE operations. Critics have pointed to persistent academic setbacks as evidence the union’s leadership should be focused on education, while AFT describes political activism and broader civil-rights advocacy as part of its mission alongside public education. Fox News Digital also reached out to the Department of Education for comment.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton unveils first endorsement in House, Senate midterm races
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Wednesday endorsed Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) in her bid for the Senate, marking the former first lady’s first endorsement of a House or Senate candidate in 2026. Flanagan wrote on social media that she was honored to have Clinton’s support, saying she “has spent five decades…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Wednesday endorsed Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) in her bid for the Senate, marking the former first lady’s first endorsement of a House or Senate candidate in 2026.

Flanagan wrote on social media that she was honored to have Clinton’s support, saying she “has spent five decades fighting for working families, dedicating her career to making the case that every child in this country deserves a fair shot.”

“Minnesota, you have an opportunity to select an extraordinary person and public servant as your next U.S. senator,” Clinton replied on Bluesky . “Please take it!”

The Hill has reached out to Clinton’s office for comment.

Clinton praised Flanagan for her “career fighting for children and families, from the Children’s Defense Fund to the Lieutenant Governor’s office, and she’s delivered for them,” according to a statement obtained by The Washington Sun . She said Flanagan will “be that same champion” if she wins her Senate bid.

Like Flanagan, Clinton worked with the Children’s Defense Fund at the start of her career. Flanagan was the executive director of the Minnesota chapter until 2015, when she was elected to Minnesota’s House of Representatives.

The endorsement also touched on President Trump’s response to rising prices, with the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran driving up the cost of gas.

“Donald Trump has made it harder for families to afford childcare, groceries and healthcare for their kids,” Clinton said, criticizing her former 2016 presidential opponent. “His tariffs and war in Iran are driving up prices, and his budget ripped healthcare and food assistance away from children so billionaires could get another tax cut.”

The Huffington Post first reported the endorsement.

Flanagan’s received a wave of endorsements from progressive lawmakers, including Clinton’s former opponent for the 2016 Democratic nomination, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), as well as Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) and Massachusetts Democratic Sens. Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren.

Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s partner election handicapper, estimates Flanagan has an 84 percent probability of winning her Senate race against Republican Michele Tafoya, who holds a 16 percent probability.

Clinton’s support brings another major voice from the Democratic Party’s past into the party’s fight to retake the House and the Senate in November.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who has also endorsed a slew of candidates, last month campaigned with Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D). The candidate is slated to have former President Obama join him on the campaign trail in Detroit later this month . Obama has also endorsed other candidates , including Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek.

articles.body:
President Trump will bring his red state campaign tour to Tennessee on Saturday to headline a rally in Clarksville.

The Republican National Committee announced Trump’s stop in Tennessee, which comes just weeks after he attended the Texas-Tennessee college football game in Knoxville.

Tennessee is home to solidly Republican gubernatorial and Senate races.

Earlier this week, Trump traveled to ruby red Nebraska to campaign for incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), who is facing an increasingly competitive reelection bid. Trump rallied in Oklahoma and Alabama last week.

After Saturday’s rally, Trump is scheduled to travel to Tuscaloosa, Ala., for the Georgia-Alabama game. However, the president told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday that his attendance will depend on the weather as Tropical Storm Isaias threatens the Gulf region.

“If there’s an emergency, if there’s a hurricane, I don’t want to do anything to take the focus off all of the great people that work in those things,” he said.

Trump’s move to visit a number of red states comes as Republicans face uphill battles in other races across the country. Trump said last week that he is visiting red states as “a sign of respect.”

The president has recently visited other competitive states as well including Texas and Ohio.

“I could have done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could have done very, very bad things to Joe Biden,” Trump said after he was asked what Democrats would impeach him for if the party wins back the House and the Senate in November.

“I could have done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama. I thought it was inappropriate to do so because you have to treat the office of the presidency with respect,” he continued, referring to the presidency as “sacred.”

Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) have told Republican voters that Democrats will impeach the president if they win the midterms.

The president was impeached twice during his first term in office. Trump was first impeached in response to a call to Ukrainian President Zelensky in which he pressured Ukraine to investigate Biden. He was later impeached following the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

Trump told reporters that Democrats do not know what they would impeach him for if they win back Congress in November.

articles.title: 2027 Super Bowl to stream on Disney+
articles.summary: Disney is betting big on streaming as the company gets set to air the Super Bowl next year in Los Angeles. The NFL’s championship game will air on Disney+, the media conglomerate’s flagship digital subscription platform, as its main television network ABC and sports arm ESPN broadcast the game on linear channels. This will be…
articles.body:
Disney is betting big on streaming as the company gets set to air the Super Bowl next year in Los Angeles.

The NFL’s championship game will air on Disney+, the media conglomerate’s flagship digital subscription platform, as its main television network ABC and sports arm ESPN broadcast the game on linear channels.

This will be the first time ESPN has ever broadcast the Super Bowl, which each season earns the largest single-night television audience of the year and reaps the host network billions in advertising revenue.

Disney putting the Feb. 14, 2027, game on its top streaming platform will make it available in more than 55 international markets, including Spanish-speaking Latin America, Brazil, the Caribbean, South Africa and Australia and New Zealand.

The NFL has made a major push into these markets in recent years, hosting more games overseas this season than any year prior.

ESPN will, as a test run, broadcast two “Monday Night Football” games on Disney+ in the weeks leading up to the Super Bowl, including a Week 7 tilt between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles.

Disney is one of several major legacy media companies that have poured millions into live streamed sports as major tech companies like Netflix, Amazon and Apple get more aggressive in the sector.

Last year’s Super Bowl, broadcast on NBC and its streamer Peacock, was watched by more than 125 million around the world and was also believed to be the most-streamed Super Bowl in history.

articles.title: Tillis says McConnell’s brain is ‘as sharp as it ever was’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Tuesday that Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) brain “is as sharp as it ever was” following the Kentucky Republican’s recent months-long absence from the upper chamber after a fall. “The difference between the [former President] Biden situation and the Mitch situation is I’ve had conversations with Mitch,” Tillis told MS NOW’s…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Tuesday that Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) brain “is as sharp as it ever was” following the Kentucky Republican’s recent months-long absence from the upper chamber after a fall.

“The difference between the [former President] Biden situation and the Mitch situation is I’ve had conversations with Mitch,” Tillis told MS NOW’s Peter Alexander on “State of Play,” referencing the former president, who also faced concerns about his age, health and ability to do his job.

“That man’s brain is as sharp as it ever was,” the North Carolina senator added. “His body’s failing him because he’s had a lifelong struggle with polio. Now, people are telling me, when I can have a coherent discussion with him — I met with him a week or so, a couple of weeks ago — ‘Mitch, how are you doing?’ He spent probably less than 30 seconds talking about that, and he immediately jumped to, ‘What are we going to do to help Ukraine? ‘What are we going to do to save the Senate and keep the filibuster?’”

Last month, McConnell, 84, returned to the Senate to cast his first vote since mid-June following months away from Capitol Hill recovering from a fall that occurred at home.

The Kentucky Republican’s extended absence and slow drips of information from his office on his condition resulted in weeks of speculation about his health and whether he would come back to the upper chamber prior to the end of his term next year.

McConnell’s time away from the Senate and advanced age refreshed conversations about lawmakers being in office for too long. Polls have shown many voters back term limits.

McConnell, now an infamous fixture of Washington, was first elected to the Senate in 1985 and is one of the longest-serving senators in American history. He is not running for reelection, with his term ending in January.

articles.title: Fetterman more popular with Pennsylvania Republicans than Democrats: Poll
articles.summary: A new poll found Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) is more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans over Democrats following his virtual appearance at the GOP’s midterm convention in September. The Quinnipiac University poll, released Wednesday, found 72 percent of Pennsylvania Republicans held a favorable opinion on Fetterman, 19 percent viewed the senator negatively, and 7 percent said…
articles.body:
A new poll found Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) is more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans over Democrats following his virtual appearance at the GOP’s midterm convention in September.

The Quinnipiac University poll , released Wednesday, found 72 percent of Pennsylvania Republicans held a favorable opinion on Fetterman, 19 percent viewed the senator negatively, and 7 percent said they had not heard enough about him.

Among the state’s Democrats, only 13 percent have a favorable opinion on him, while 69 percent do not have a favorable opinion, and 15 percent have not heard enough about him. Among Pennsylvania independents, 27 percent held a favorable opinion of Fetterman, 49 percent had an unfavorable opinion, and 23 percent had not heard enough about him.

Though the Keystone State senator has voted with the Democratic caucus 90 percent of the time, he split from his party on several high-profile votes — including helping Republicans block a Senate war powers resolution. These departures — along with his midterm convention appearance — have caused many to question Fetterman’s party loyalty.

Fetterman also voted with GOP lawmakers against cutting off aid to Israel, even saying previously at the Hill Nation Summit he would leave the Democratic Party if it turned its back on the country entirely — though he has repeatedly asserted he will not “be a Republican.”

Even GOP Sen. Dave McCormick (Pa.) is notably less popular among Pennsylvania Republicans compared to Fetterman, as 67 percent felt favorably about McCormick in Wednesday’s poll, 13 percent do not have a favorable opinion, and 20 percent did not know enough about him.

Out of all likely Pennsylvania voters surveyed, 37 percent reported holding favorable opinions of Fetterman, while 46 percent had an unfavorable view, and 15 percent haven’t heard enough about him.

His Democratic colleagues in Congress similarly grew frustrated with Fetterman following his video appearance at the Republican midterm convention, in which he introduced McCormick and described him as a “great friend.”

Fetterman said in a statement after the video’s release that he would continue to caucus with Democrats, writing, “I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party — and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”

His seat is not up for reelection until 2028, and he has repeatedly asked reporters to “just wait” until the midterms when asked about his future with the party.

“And if I turn a Republican, then I’ll be a liar … My name is not on the ballot. Chill,” Fetterman said in mid-September.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and a number of other Republican senators have stated they would welcome Fetterman to the GOP.

The poll was conducted between Oct. 1 – 5 among 1,159 likely voters in Pennsylvania. The margin of error is 3.9 percentage points.

articles.title: House Republican defends GOP ahead of midterms: ‘We did our job’
articles.summary: Georgia Rep. Buddy Carter (R) defended the Republican Party’s strategy ahead of the midterm elections, as President Trump urges Americans to cast their vote as if he were “on the ballot.” CNN’s Jake Tapper questioned Carter on Tuesday about the effectiveness of the president’s message this election cycle, in which his party is fighting to…
articles.body:
Georgia Rep. Buddy Carter (R) defended the Republican Party’s strategy ahead of the midterm elections, as President Trump urges Americans to cast their vote as if he were “ on the ballot .”

CNN’s Jake Tapper questioned Carter on Tuesday about the effectiveness of the president’s message this election cycle, in which his party is fighting to maintain control of both chambers of Congress.

“I think he’s got the right strategy,” the GOP lawmaker said. “Look, we’ve got a record to run on. We changed America after the Biden-Harris administration, and we did our job.

“We secured the border, we made sure Americans are safer, we make sure we’ve got a robust economy,” he continued. “All of those things are things we need to be running on.”

Carter also addressed the public discontent around the Trump administration’s ongoing military operation in Iran — primarily rising energy and cost of living expenses tied to the conflict. A Marquette Law School Supreme Court poll from August found that 75 percent of respondents did not believe these military operations were “worth the cost.”

The average price of standard fuel was up by more than a dollar per gallon from a year ago Wednesday, according to AAA . In Georgia alone, the price of gas increased by just shy of a dollar in the same period.

The president has brushed aside concerns about the increased costs as a “very inexpensive price to pay” for the war.

Carter said there was “no question” that gas prices are “too high,” but he praised the U.S.’s ongoing military operation against Tehran.

“He is making this country safer by making sure that Iran doesn’t have a nuclear bomb, by making sure they don’t have ballistic missiles that can reach our homeland,” the Georgia Republican said. “All of those things are vitally important — we have to keep that in mind.”

The lawmaker ran in the GOP primary in Georgia’s U.S. Senate race, but he was defeated by Trump-backed Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.).

When asked about his expectations for the closely watched November match-up between Collins and incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), he said, “this race is still going to tighten up.”

“I think that this is going to get tighter as we get closer to Election Day,” Carter added.

Recent polling has shown Ossoff with a marked advantage in the race, leading by between 4 points and 11 points in recent surveys.

articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday his administration’s new investment accounts for children will have a “huge effect” in reducing positive views of socialism and communism among young Americans.

During an event in the Oval Office promoting the “ Trump Accounts ,” the president said children will be “watching their accounts” grow until gaining control over them upon turning 18.

Children will now be automatically enrolled in the initiative, which the administration created under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Trump signed into law in July 2025.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The auto-enrollment will result in more than 60 million additional kids having an account, per the Treasury Department. The president said Wednesday that nearly 8 million children already have an account.

“Long term, I think it’ll have a huge effect on … [views of] socialism, communism,” Trump predicted. “This is really the alternative, and it’s a great alternative.”

Children born from the start of 2025 through 2028 will receive $1,000 from the federal government in their accounts, though parents must first claim the child’s auto-enrolled Trump Account to receive the contribution.

Once the child turns 18, their account will function as a traditional individual retirement account.

The federal government will also invest the accounts in one of five low-cost exchange-traded funds, which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said will contribute to young Americans learning about the stock market.

“I think this is going to be a real-time financial literacy project,” Bessent said in the Oval Office.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who was at the White House for the event, said the accounts will be one of the “biggest parts” of Trump’s legacy.

“We are creating a whole new generation of capitalists,” the Texas Republican remarked.

The president and GOP lawmakers have attacked Democrats over the recent crop of left-wing candidates winning primaries across the country , claiming it is evidence of a “communist” takeover of the party.

According to a recent Gallup poll , 43 percent of Americans surveyed had a positive view of socialism — the highest mark the firm has seen since 2010. Among respondents ages 18-34, 57 percent viewed socialism positively.

He was arrested Tuesday in a public park following the purchase.

FBI Director Kash Patel also celebrated the foil.

articles.body:
President Trump dismissed a question Wednesday about his administration sending money to Americans ahead of the midterms, choosing instead to tout his tariffs.

“What we’re doing is we have tremendous growth. We have the greatest growth of any country, maybe ever in history,” the president said in the Oval Office , when the Independent’s Andrew Feinberg asked whether he was sending money to Americans “in hopes they vote for” Republicans.

“We’re able to do this that the Democrats can’t, because they would’ve not … been able to use tariffs so wisely like we did,” Trump added.

Trump last month pledged to send $5,000 to every American adult if the GOP retains control of Congress in the midterms.

“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” he said at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas.

The president also said last week his administration will send $90 to more than 20 million seniors to offset Medicare Part B premium costs.

That came after the administration began mailing $500 refund checks to about 1 million Americans who it says were overcharged for their Affordable Care Act insurance.

While multiple Republican lawmakers came out against the $5,000 dividend proposal, the president doubled down later in the month, saying the $5,000 dividends will “100 percent” happen .

Republicans hold slim majorities in the Senate and House. But Decision Desk HQ , The Hill’s data partner, gives Democrats a 54 percent chance to flip both chambers in November.

If the federal government sent $5,000 to each of the roughly 270 million U.S. adults, it would cost more than $1 trillion.

Republican politicians who opposed the proposal , including Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) and outgoing Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), cited the ballooning national debt for why the country cannot afford it.

The national debt exceeded $40 trillion for the first time in August and sits at more than $40.2 trillion as of Monday.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told NBC News last month the administration will not fund the dividends using taxpayer dollars .

Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council, told Bloomberg TV in September that Congress can authorize the checks via reconciliation, which would allow Republicans to bypass Democrats.

articles.title: Attorneys describe Christa Pike’s emotional reaction after waking up
articles.summary: On Monday night, Pike’s legal team was told that Pike was braindead, and life support would be removed. But Pike woke up on Tuesday and began speaking.
articles.body:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. ( WKRN ) — Christa Pike’s defense attorneys on Wednesday described their client’s emotional state after discovering she was still alive following a botched execution attempt .

On Monday night, Pike’s legal team was told she was braindead, and life support would be removed the next day. However, to their surprise, their client woke up on Tuesday and began speaking.

According to one of her attorneys, the first thing the inmate said when she woke up was, “Where am I, and who are you?” He added there is still a lot of cognitive confusion, but Pike has allegedly asked about several people, including the victim’s family.

“I think she is angry and confused about everything right now,” said defense lawyer Randy Spivey during a press conference. “She is very aware that the state tried to execute her, and, again, I don’t want to say what she remembers and what she doesn’t remember at this point because I think that is evolving.”

Her legal team added that she likely has pneumonia and is not able to swallow, so she has not eaten. They also noted that both of the inmate’s arms and hands are “tremendously swollen.” Spivey described them as looking like a “blown up surgical glove.”

Pike’s lawyers emphasized they have not asked the state to turn over any evidence but rather preserve it, so the public can really learn what happened on Sept. 30, Spivey said.

“Today’s hearing was just the first step of many to preserve and enforce Christa’s Constitutional rights after this unprecedented, botched execution,” the attorney added.

Pike is alive and speaking nearly a week after she was given two lethal injection doses during the failed execution attempt, her attorneys confirmed Tuesday.

Earlier this week, Pike remained incapacitated on a ventilator while medical staff worked to clear the drug from her system. However, by Tuesday, Oct. 6, Pike’s attorneys said she was conscious, speaking and receiving critical medical care.

Pike’s attorneys noted that she sustained “severe damage” to her arms and remains handcuffed and shackled to a hospital bed. Although her prognosis remains unclear, the legal team said, at minimum, they expect a “long recovery.”

“Christa is a survivor. She survived child sexual abuse; she survived rapes of multiple men; she survived a suicide attempt when she was 12, and she survived the state’s attempt to execute her,” Spivey said.

Court rules to preserve evidence from execution attempt

Before the press conference, a status hearing was also held in Nashville court on the preservation of evidence from Tennessee’s failed execution.

Pike’s attorneys were granted the expedited hearing Friday to discuss the preservation of relevant evidence after they filed an emergency motion. The beginning of the hearing focused on jurisdiction of the case, with Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles deciding her court still has current jurisdiction.

Ultimately, Chancellor Myles determined her court will issue a new order to save every piece of potential evidence from the execution chamber that might need to be preserved and maintained. This includes pictures, remnants of drugs, anything in the witness room, handwritten notes, logs and witness accounts, in addition to all pertinent emails, texts and recordings.

“In light of the evolving situation, the court will grant its own order, granting the motion to preserve relevant evidence. As a primary order, we want all drugs, IV, syringes, tubing, anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained. That would include waste,” explained Chancellor Myles.

“Anything pertaining to the actual drug that was used needs to be maintained and preserved, as well as any supplies that would have come from the manufacture administering those products.”

Pike’s attorneys stated that since her hospitalization, Pike has remained shackled to her bed. Medical staff has asked for her to not be restrained and those requests were denied.

The attorneys claim they were able to access Pike until Monday after a two-and-a-half hour wait at the hospital. They asked the judge to grant them similar access to what they had when she was in prison.

The state argued the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) doesn’t intend to obstruct Pike’s attorneys’ access to her, and access is being facilitated: The judge ordered Pike’s attorneys to send requests to prison wardens to request a visit with Pike two hours prior. Wardens must then respond within those two hours.

Chancellor Myles is waiting to decide whether Pike can use a tablet she used in prison until she gets more information.

“The court will reserve ruling on the tablet for Ms. Pike while she is in a private hospital,” Myles said.

After the hearing, Pike’s attorneys held a press conference on her condition.

“We have to ask how much suffering is enough. We continue to ask Gov. Lee to commute Christa’s death sentence. After all we have seen and all we still do not know, it is unimaginable that the state would try to execute her again,” said Spivey

Pike was convicted of brutally killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville in 1995 when she was 18. She would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

This is the second time in 2026 that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution: In May, state officials called off the execution of Tony Carruthers after executioners failed to place an IV to administer the injection. He remains on death row after Lee granted a one-year reprieve.

Gov. Bill Lee (R) demanded a review of the state’s execution procedures and has indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution. He also delayed the remaining execution this year for Gary Wayne Sutton, who was scheduled to be put to death on Dec. 3, 2026.

articles.title: Unearthed clip exposes how far Talarico was willing to go on raising taxes during COVID era
articles.summary: James Talarico once said he didn't care what taxes had to be raised to avoid healthcare cuts in Texas during the COVID-19 budget shortfalls.
articles.body: James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for the Senate in Texas, once pressed Democrats to consider cuts to healthcare benefits a nonstarter — regardless of the consequences for the state’s finances. The remark came during a podcast interview in which Talarico discussed how Texas might balance its budget amid COVID-related shortfalls. He feared Republicans would look for savings in healthcare services. "I don't care where you get the revenue. I don't care what taxes you have to raise," Talarico said in a 2020 appearance with Texas Rising, a progressive YouTube channel focused on political engagement among younger voters. The resurfaced moment adds to the pile of past statements dealing with gender, immigration and fiscal management, complicating the political calculus for Talarico as he aims to convince voters in Texas that he could represent a Republican-leaning constituency, even as a Democrat. TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS At the time, Texas was facing a bleak financial outlook. The pandemic had crippled key sections of the state’s regular revenue streams. As oil demand crashed nationally, tax revenue that would normally come from hotels, bars and restaurants also faced steep reductions. Texas Comptroller Glenn Hegar projected a $4.6 billion shortfall. "The economic contraction associated with COVID-19 has resulted in revenue collection this fiscal year that is much lower than our earlier projections," Hegar said in a statement. "This estimate also assumes that restrictions on businesses and individuals will be lifted before the end of this calendar year and that economic activity will strengthen." As a part of the COVID response, Texas ordered most agencies to look for ways to cut their spending by 5% in the 2020 – 2021 budget. In a letter, Governor Greg Abbott largely shielded Health and Human Services (HHS) from the reductions, sparing the state’s Medicaid program, the Children’s Health Insurance Program, the foster care program and disability services, among others. Even so, $2.6 billion of HHS’s budget remained subject to cuts, according to the agency's estimations. That left the Health and Human Services Commission with a target of $132,716,600 in cuts. 'FAKE' MODERATE TALARICO'S TEXAS SURGE TESTS PAXTON IN FIGHT TO HOLD CRUCIAL GOP SENATE SEAT Despite the reduced figure, Talarico blasted the idea of making spending reductions geared towards healthcare. "You're not going to make our students and our teachers — you're not going to make the sick and the elderly pay for this pandemic we are not going to balance our budget off of the most vulnerable people in this state," Talarico said. He argued that Democrats should create a similar kind of stigma against cuts to HHS as the one surrounding raising taxes. "Sometimes you get the reaction in the capitol that's an unreasonable position to take. But the other side of the aisle has already taken revenue increases off the table. They've done a good job of making certain options taboo, so I think our coalition, not just Democrats but progressives, and anybody with a functioning heart should be able to make cuts to health and education taboo and take them off the table," Talarico said. The moment has brought on criticisms from at least one Republican onlooker. "High-tax Talarico never saw a tax hike he didn't love in the Texas Legislature, and he is promising to continue that if elected to the Senate. James Talarico will raise taxes on every Texan to fund his radical agenda of taxpayer-funded sex changes for kids and free healthcare for illegal immigrants," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee said in a statement to Fox News Digital. As he wages his bid for U.S. Senate, Talarico has advocated for an expansion of U.S. health policy. On his website, Talarico has called for universal eligibility for Medicare, to regulate medical debt and expand veteran care. His views on Medicare, which overlap with many other progressives in the party, have prompted criticism from Republicans who believe such an expansion would cripple the federal budget with cost. Skeptics of the plan have argued for years that such an expansion is too expensive and does little to address existing inefficiencies in the American healthcare system. In 2019, Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., took to the Senate floor to blast the idea, calling it a straitjacket solution that would undermine healthcare quality. "The [Congressional Budget Office] projects in its report on a single-payer plan that government spending on health care would increase substantially. They go on to say to cover the massive cost of government-run care, income taxes would have to at least double. Income taxes, American families — at least double," Barrasso said. SHOCK POLL: TALARICO TIES PAXTON IN TEXAS SENATE RACE, THREATENING GOP STRONGHOLD Talarico’s campaign did not address questions on whether his designs for healthcare are shaped by the national deficit, but noted that his plan includes increases in taxes on the country's top earners. "James supports making billionaires pay their fair share so we can cut taxes for middle class Texans and fund healthcare for working families — which is why he has unveiled plans to end special tax handouts to corporations and billionaires to help fund healthcare, while proudly voting for the largest property tax cut in Texas history to make sure middle class families get a break," the Talarico campaign told Fox News Digital. "Ken Paxton has worked to enrich himself and his billionaire mega-donors, amassed 15 properties on a taxpayer-funded salary, and was impeached by his own party for his corrupt abuse of office." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Having cleared the party primary, Talarico will face off against Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton in the state’s Nov. 3 general election.

articles.title: Half of Democratic voters say the party will win Congress because of Trump’s actions: Poll
articles.summary: Half of Democratic voters say they expect their party to retake the House and Senate in the November midterm elections, mostly in response to President Trump’s policies and actions, according to a poll released Wednesday. A Politico poll found that 50 percent of Democratic respondents believed their party will take over the House and Senate…
articles.body:
Half of Democratic voters say they expect their party to retake the House and Senate in the November midterm elections, mostly in response to President Trump’s policies and actions, according to a poll released Wednesday.

A Politico poll found that 50 percent of Democratic respondents believed their party will take over the House and Senate due to Trump’s actions, compared with 35 percent who said the party will claim Congress because candidates ran strong campaigns.

Forty-six percent said they will vote to oppose Trump, and 37 percent said they’ll vote to support a candidate in their area.

Conversely, 41 percent of MAGA-aligned voters said Republicans will lose both chambers only if they run weak campaigns, and 22 percent said it will be because of Trump’s actions.

The poll showed that 43 percent of Democratic midterm voters believed the blame would be on Democratic candidates for running weak campaigns should Republicans maintain control of both chambers of Congress. Another 22 percent said it would happen based on Trump’s actions.

Among MAGA-aligned voters, 37 percent said they would credit Trump’s actions, and 36 percent said they would credit strong Republican campaigns if the GOP keeps control of Congress. Another 17 percent told pollsters GOP control of Congress will be the result of weak Democratic campaigns.

Slightly more non-MAGA Trump voters said the GOP’s loss of Congress would be because of Trump’s actions (31 percent) and weak Republican campaigns (29 percent), while nearly a quarter said it would be because of strong Democratic campaigns.

Forty percent said the GOP keeping its majority in both chambers would likely be based on strong Republican campaigns, while 22 percent said it would be because of Trump’s actions and 25 percent said it would be because Democrats campaigned poorly.

“Trump is getting his wish: The president is, in effect, on the ballot and remains the main character of this election cycle,” Politico wrote about its poll findings. “That’s causing major headwinds for GOP candidates, who already face an incumbent disadvantage from voters who historically seek change from the party in power.”

“Trump’s approval rating is historically low, and polls suggest voters blame him for the affordability crisis at the center of both parties’ messaging,” the outlet added.

Trump and other Republican lawmakers predict Democrats will seek to impeach the president if they gain control of Congress — a possibility that some Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), have not ruled out .

“It’s guaranteed, probably on the first day — first or second day,” House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Tuesday in an interview with Scott Jennings, a pro-Trump pundit. “Remember, they’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress. And they’re raring to go.”

The Politico survey was conducted Oct. 3-5 and included 2,001 respondents with a margin of error of 2.2 percentage points.

articles.title: US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
articles.summary: A Gallup survey highlights a deep – and historic – partisan divide over confidence in the country’s elections.
articles.body:
With less than a month to go before the United States’ pivotal midterms, a new survey found that most independent voters and supporters of President Donald Trump’s Republican Party do not believe the elections will be honest.

Polling from Gallup, released on Wednesday, found 37 percent of Republicans and 35 percent of independents have confidence in the country’s electoral system, significantly lower than US Democrats (63 percent).

Overall, 49 percent of Americans said they were confident in the honesty of elections, while 51 percent said they were not. Those figures are unchanged from the country’s last midterm election in 2022.

This “marks a change from 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, when confidence was nominally higher among approvers (51 percent) than disapprovers (45 percent)”, Gallup wrote in a statement highlighting the results of the survey.

The numbers highlight a deep, historic partisan divide over confidence in US elections.

“Since 2025 and Trump’s return to the White House, the relationship between leadership approval and confidence in elections has disappeared,” Gallup wrote.

Gallup said that the US is the only country out of more than 100 polled annually over the past 15 years to show this pattern – trust in US election integrity is markedly higher among those who disapprove of the country’s leadership under Trump (52 percent) than those who approve (41 percent).

In more than 100 countries where the polling organisation tracks views of national leadership and confidence in elections, people who approve of their governments have generally been more likely to trust their country’s elections.

In 2025, 70 percent of people globally who approved of their national leadership expressed confidence in the honesty of their elections, compared with 30 percent among those who disapproved.

“The current US pattern is highly unusual compared with the rest of the world,” Gallup wrote.

Under former US President Joe Biden, 81 percent of Americans who approved of the government expressed confidence in elections, compared with just 30 percent of those who disapproved, according to Gallup.

Gallup said the unusual divide could have implications for the November elections, raising questions about whether some voters will view the results as legitimate.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Jackson, Collins tangle on Canada tariffs: ‘We can’t eat road salt’
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Democrat Troy Jackson tangled over the Trump administration’s tariffs on Canada during the first debate of their battleground Senate race in Maine. Collins stressed her opposition to the tariffs on Canada, hailing America’s longtime ally as a vital trading partner for the state she’s represented for five terms in the…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Democrat Troy Jackson tangled over the Trump administration’s tariffs on Canada during the first debate of their battleground Senate race in Maine.

Collins stressed her opposition to the tariffs on Canada, hailing America’s longtime ally as a vital trading partner for the state she’s represented for five terms in the Senate.

“But I’ve also been working behind the scenes. Troy mocked it, but I was successful in getting concrete, pulp and road salt removed from the tariff list. And if you ask towns in northern Maine and eastern Maine, they get all of their road salt from Canada,” the senator said.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

She sent a letter in August to the administration on the “unfortunate breakdown in trade negotiations” between the U.S. and Canada that resulted in tariffs, and urged the administration to consider that “Maine’s economy is uniquely intertwined with Canada,” with a 611-mile shared border. The exemptions were announced in September .

“I didn’t mock the fact that she got road salt back. I mock the fact that: What about everything else? I mean, we can’t eat road salt,” Jackson hit back at the debate.

The Democrat argued that, in light of the Iran war and other factors driving up prices, “There’s going to be so many less people to be able to afford to drive that I’m not even sure the road salt’s going to be worth anything either.”

Democrats quickly seized on the exchange, with the party’s Senate campaign arm likening Collins’s comment to Marie Antoinette’s infamous “let them eat cake” line.

Republicans’ Senate campaign arm, on the other hand, cast blame for Maine’s economic struggles on Jackson’s 20-year tenure in the state Legislature.

The hourlong debate hosted by WGME-TV was the first of four scheduled faceoffs between Collins and Jackson as Election Day nears.

Jackson has been leading Collins by roughly a point in Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages of the race, and top forecasters rate the race as a critical toss-up in the fight for Senate control.
