articles.title: Watch live: Trump rallies Texas Republicans amid midterm warning signs
articles.summary: President Trump is returning to Texas Wednesday night as Republicans look to shore up support in an increasingly competitive midterm landscape. Trump will rally voters in San Antonio, marking his third trip to the state in a month after stops in Dallas for the GOP midterm convention and a tour last week at a truck…
articles.body:
President Trump is returning to Texas Wednesday night as Republicans look to shore up support in an increasingly competitive midterm landscape.

Trump will rally voters in San Antonio, marking his third trip to the state in a month after stops in Dallas for the GOP midterm convention and a tour last week at a truck facility in Denton.

The latest visit comes as polls show Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton trailing Democrat James Talarico in the race to replace outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R). Once seen as a GOP stronghold, multiple forecasters now view the seat as a toss-up.

Paxton is expected to join Trump at the rally, along with Republican House candidate Carlos De La Cruz, who is locked in another competitive race in the Lone Star State’s redrawn 35th Congressional District. The House hopeful is the brother of Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R), who is running for reelection in the state’s 15th District.

The stop is the latest in the president’s swing through red states as the party fights to maintain the majority of Congress next term.

His remarks are scheduled to begin at 7 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: DNC sues to block Trump administration from using government funds for political ads
articles.summary: The Democratic National Committee (DNC) on Wednesday sued the Trump administration, claiming it misused congressional appropriations in using government funding to run new ads featuring the president. “The Trump Administration is using taxpayer dollars to air political advertisements, a blatant violation of the statutory ban on the use of appropriations for ‘publicity or propaganda purposes.’…
articles.body:
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) on Wednesday sued the Trump administration, claiming it misused congressional appropriations in using government funding to run new ads featuring the president.

“The Trump Administration is using taxpayer dollars to air political advertisements, a blatant violation of the statutory ban on the use of appropriations for ‘publicity or propaganda purposes.’ President Trump personally directed this illegal activity,” the DNC claims in the suit.

“The Trump Administration’s illegal use of taxpayer dollars for campaign-style advertisements deprives the DNC of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates. The use of public funds also places the DNC and Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage, even though the publicly funded propaganda advertisements are deeply unpopular with American voters, by preserving funds held by campaign committees and PACs—including MAGA Inc.—for other political expenditures.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The suit asks the court to enjoin the ads, blocking the administration from continuing to use government funds to run them.

Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, one of which features the song “Love Me” by artist JMSN, who said the song was used without his permission.

The 30-second ad shows numerous images of the president overlaid by quotes from recent speeches demeaning communism while also crediting himself for the largest tax cuts in history.

The ads have been paid for through funding earmarked for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Trump on Monday reserved course , saying he would use his own political fundraising dollars to continue to pay for the ads.

But the suit notes that, thus far, that has not happened.

“Yet for the next two days, the ads have continued to air, still labeled ‘Paid for by the U.S. Government,’” the DNC wrote in its suit.

In response to a request for comment on Wednesday’s suit, the White House referred The Hill to Trump’s Monday pledge to fund the ads himself.

The White House has said Trump does not plan to reimburse the government for the $10 million already spent on the ad.

The suit from the DNC comes after the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington filed a complaint with the Department of Homeland Security Inspector General asserting that the ad campaign violated numerous laws, including the Antideficiency Act, the Purpose Statute and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, each of which place limitations on how federal funding can be spent.

“The propaganda ads marshal government resources in support of the President’s party in advance of the 2026 midterm election. This use of Congressional appropriations for partisan purposes violates the clear command of federal law. Fundamentally, the ads undermine free and fair elections,” it wrote.

The suit references other ads in the series prepared for the president beyond the “Love Me” ad, including those referencing the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, another in which Trump pledges to “demolish the Deep State,” and others featuring Mount Rushmore and promoting America’s military power.

Another component of the suit is the harm to the DNC, framing itself as a direct competitor to Trump’s efforts.

“The Trump Administration has continued to air the ads at public expense and preserved MAGA Inc.’s funds for other political efforts adverse to Democratic candidates and the DNC,” they said, referencing Trump’s political action committee that has otherwise spent $25 million campaigning for Republicans or against Democrats.

“This alters campaign spending rules in ways that deprive ‘candidate[s] of a fair process.'”

articles.title: Lawyers looking to block Texas man’s execution following Christa Pike’s botched execution
articles.summary: Lawyers for a Texas death row inmate are looking to block his execution following the botched lethal injection attempts against Christa Pike in Tennessee. Jamaal Howard is scheduled for execution by lethal injection on Oct. 7 at 7 p.m. EDT, marking the first time an inmate has been put to death since the incident with…
articles.body:
Lawyers for a Texas death row inmate are looking to block his execution following the botched lethal injection attempts against Christa Pike in Tennessee.

Jamaal Howard is scheduled for execution by lethal injection on Oct. 7 at 7 p.m. EDT, marking the first time an inmate has been put to death since the incident with Pike — who is still alive days after the state’s failed attempts to execute her. His lawyers are looking to stop the execution, citing Texas’s drug of choice — pentobarbital — which was also used in Pike’s two botched injections, according to The Associated Press .

Howard’s lawyers also said they believed the state’s drug supply had become degraded in their appeal to the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals.

On Sept. 30, Pike received two doses of pentobarbital and survived. She was taken from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in an ambulance to a Nashville-area hospital. Her legal team said Tuesday she was alive and speaking following the lethal doses but sustained “severe damage” to her arms.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) ordered that Pike’s execution be delayed until at least next year.

Howard was found guilty of capital murder for killing Vickie Swartout in 2000, when he was 20, during an attempted robbery. According to court filings, Howard took $114 and cigarettes from a store, located about 100 miles north of Houston.

Attorneys for Howard previously appealed the execution to the Supreme Court, arguing that he is mentally disabled and thus ineligible for the death penalty.

“No court has ever decided whether Howard is intellectually disabled under the clinical standards that govern today,” his lawyers wrote in the appeal . “Under those standards, his full-scale IQ of 74 and the sworn testimony from his 2001 trial describing his adaptive deficits at ages 20 and 21 make far more than the threshold showing required to have his claim heard.”

In 2002, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Atkins v. Virginia that executing inmates with mental disabilities was unconstitutional, though the court left it up to the states to determine who qualifies as disabled. In another case, the court invalidated a Florida law that determined mental disability using an IQ thresholding.

The Death Penalty Information Center estimates there have been at least 64 instances of botched executions across the U.S. since 1982 — 10 of which were in Texas.

articles.title: DNC lawsuit accuses Trump administration of diverting $20M in federal funds for 'propaganda' ads
articles.summary: The Democratic National Committee alleges the Trump administration directed $20 million in taxpayer funds toward ads designed to boost Republicans ahead of 2026 midterms.
articles.body: The Democratic National Committee is suing the Trump administration, alleging it illegally diverted $20 million in federal funds to produce and broadcast partisan political advertisements. The ad campaign was designed to boost Republican prospects in the upcoming 2026 midterm elections and shore up President Donald Trump’s approval ratings, a move the DNC argues constitutes unlawful "publicity or propaganda," the lawsuit states. The lawsuit claims President Donald Trump personally directed the campaign, violating the longstanding statutory ban on using federal appropriations for "publicity or propaganda purposes." REPUBLICAN PARTY TO HOST HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION IN DALLAS, TRUMP ANNOUNCES ON TRUTH SOCIAL "President Trump’s political propaganda ads are an attempt to resuscitate his historically low approval ratings and avoid widespread Republican defeats in the 2026 midterm election," the lawsuit states. "The President has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day ‘midterm convention,’ and repeatedly directed voters to ‘pretend that I am on the ballot.’" The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) transferred the funds from money authorized under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to court filings. 2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN The OMB approved reallocating the funds into a U.S. Customs and Border Protection line item designated for "Commemorative Events," according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit also notes that congressional committee reports explicitly restricted that line item to line-of-duty death memorials, agency anniversaries and commendation ceremonies. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump wrote on Truth Social earlier this week. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!" The lawsuit highlights mounting pressure on Republicans, noting that polling numbers have dropped in traditional battlegrounds as well as in typically conservative states, which leaves Democrats "poised to take control of Congress, governor’s mansions, and state legislatures around the country." MADURO CLAIMS IMMUNITY, ASKS JUDGE TO DISMISS DRUG-TRAFFICKING CHARGES AGAINST HIM AND HIS WIFE Among the ads flagged in the filing is one featuring President Trump touting the capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. In another spot, Trump directly addresses the audience: "With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state. We will expel the warmongers from our government. We will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists." A third ad explicitly asks viewers to "pretend I'm on the ballot" to drive turnout. The lawsuit also targets ads featuring high-ranking administration officials praising Trump, including War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "As gas and grocery costs rise and his approval numbers continue to crater, this president has stooped to taking money from a fund intended for memorials for Americans killed in the line of duty to promote his failed policies. articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s open Senate race, on Tuesday accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of pushing the Trump administration to enter the Iran war.

The ongoing conflict began when Israel and the U.S. launched joint strikes on Tehran on Feb. 28. As the war continues to stretch past the seven-month mark, global energy prices have skyrocketed because of the effective halt of commercial oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a major trading corridor in the region.

“We are in the war in Iran in part because of the advocacy of the Israeli prime minister,” the Democrat told Leland Vittert, NewsNation’s chief Washington anchor, on Tuesday.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“There’s no disagreement on that,” the Democrat continued. “He came to the Situation Room and advocated for the war, and we’re now paying … for it. Our gas, our groceries are unaffordable, and that’s on top of the billions in tax dollars that we spend sending our money over there.”

Despite starting the conflict together, President Trump said in June that his administration, and not Israel’s, called the shots in this war. The prime minister later pushed back , saying his government had “every right to self-defense” and would “exercise that right whenever necessary.”

Affordability has become a top issue this election cycle amid growing public discontent with hiked costs of living during this conflict. Seventy-five percent of respondents in a Marquette Law School Supreme Court poll from August said they believe these military operations were not “worth the cost.”

Lawmakers have successfully passed several Iran powers resolutions — including three in the House and one in the Senate — to urge the Trump administration to end U.S. military operations against Iran amid these growing tolls on U.S. consumers.

“I have been more than extremely clear about this: I don’t want our tax dollars being used to subsidize war abroad,” El-Sayed said. “I don’t want our tax dollars being used to fund, unconditionally, foreign militaries.”

The Democratic nominee will square off against his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), in a Thursday debate in Grand Rapids.

Ahead of the debate Wednesday, Rogers broke with the White House when he reversed his position on Trump’s tariffs and advocated for an immediate end to the trade fight between the U.S. and Canada. The Republican previously praised these economic policies as “necessary.”

El-Sayed accused his opponent of “flip-flopping” on this issue because he was falling behind in the polls. The Democrat has maintained a narrow lead in recent surveys among likely Michigan voters.

“Donald is the reason we’re in a trade war. And he’s the reason you’re running,” the Democrat wrote on social media Wednesday, referring to the president.

articles.title: Trump to propose relaxing oil and gas methane rules
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Trump to propose relaxing oil and gas methane rules The Trump administration plans to loosen restrictions that rein in methane from oil and gas production, it announced Wednesday. © Matthew Brown, Associated Press The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said in a press release that…
articles.body:
Trump to propose relaxing oil and gas methane rules

The Trump administration plans to loosen restrictions that rein in methane from oil and gas production, it announced Wednesday.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said in a press release that in the coming days, it will propose changes to Biden-era energy regulations .

It did not release a specific proposal but said it would make adjustments to several aspects of the Biden-era rule , including the repeal of a program that would require energy companies to respond to credible reports of major methane leaks.

The EPA also said it would propose to change regulations for a group of low-producing, high-emitting wells known as “marginal” oil and gas wells.

The agency did not detail what regulatory changes it will suggest related to these wells and did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for more information.

ProPublica reported last month , citing a draft that was under White House review, that the rule would dramatically loosen requirements for leak inspections and equipment upgrades at marginal wells, which are estimated to produce just 7 percent of the nation’s oil and gas but about half of its methane emissions.

Meanwhile, the EPA said Wednesday it would “revisit” its approach to excess gas that’s extracted alongside oil after the Biden administration sought to eliminate the burning off of this gas — known as flaring — at new wells. The EPA did not say what changes it was eyeing but that it would seek to make “compliance possible all over the country and ensure a reasonable approach.”

The EPA said in a written statement that the moves could save an estimated $45 billion.

articles.title: Texas becomes center of midterms universe
articles.summary: Texas has taken center stage ahead of next month’s midterm elections as Democrats grow more optimistic about their chances in the state up and down the ballot. For months, the state’s highly contested Senate race has dominated midterm elections headlines, but Democrats say they are seeing opportunity in other Texas contests as well. The Democratic…
articles.body:
Texas has taken center stage ahead of next month’s midterm elections as Democrats grow more optimistic about their chances in the state up and down the ballot.

For months, the state’s highly contested Senate race has dominated midterm elections headlines, but Democrats say they are seeing opportunity in other Texas contests as well. The Democratic Governors Association and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) announced this week they each plan to give $1 million to support Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the state’s gubernatorial race.

Meanwhile, leaked audio of Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton blaming the national GOP as Democrat James Talarico leads in the polls has rocked the Senate race.

Still, President Trump and Vice President Vance have traveled multiple times to the state to bolster Lone Star State Republicans in competitive contests. Trump is set to rally alongside Paxton and Republican House candidate Carlos De La Cruz in San Antonio Wednesday evening.

“Texas is clearly in play,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based GOP strategist who ran Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) 2014 reelection bid.

“Republicans understand they have a real threat they need to defend against, and Democrats see a real opportunity where they can go on offense, and potentially win a U.S. Senate seat and maybe even the governor’s race as well,” he added.

A New York Times/Siena University poll from Saturday showed Talarico with a 7 percentage point lead over Paxton, while Hinojosa edged out Texas Gov. Greg Abbott by 3 points.

“I think we waited too long to send in the cavalry,” Paxton donor Dan Eberhart said when asked about the state of the race.

On Wednesday, another leak of Paxton’s remarks from a closed-door fundraiser surfaced, with the state attorney general blaming the Iran war and high gas prices for his standing in the polls.

“It’s not tariffs. … It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” Paxton told donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser, according to audio obtained by Axios.

A spokesperson for Paxton’s campaign told the outlet that the development is a “non-story,” adding that Paxton acknowledged “what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high.”

One Republican strategist blasted Paxton’s remarks to donors as “hugely problematic.”

“Why would you say those things? I mean, it’s just unimaginable, to be honest, that you would let your guard down that much and say things that hurt your standing, the president’s standing, and frankly just feeds into an already challenging narrative,” the strategist said.

Steinhauser called the intraparty squabbling “unhelpful.”

“This is not the time to be doing that,” Steinhauser said. “I don’t want to see Republicans out there starting the blame game. I think that creates a psychology of losing. It creates a psychology of depressing turnout.”

“There definitely is sort of an undercurrent of potential blame game that’s already starting,” he added.

Other Republicans warn the Senate race’s drama could have a detrimental impact on the state’s House races, as Democrats seek to win back control of the lower chamber in November.

“It is important that Paxton wins,” Eberhart said. “A Paxton loss likely brings with it six House losses.”

Texas is home to six competitive House races this cycle in the 9th, 15th, 23rd, 28th, 34th and 35th districts.

Abbott and his Republicans sought to boost their party’s chances on the congressional map by shifting five blue seats toward Republicans via mid-decade redistricting . The strategy was replicated in other red states across the country including Florida.

However, Democrats predict their candidates are on track to fare better in the races given the poor political environment for Republicans, including Trump’s standing with Latino and Hispanic voters in the state.

“This was the first stone thrown in the gerrymander wars, and they f‑‑‑ed it up,” said one Democratic operative.

Chad Wilbanks, former executive director of the Texas Republican Party, said it’s realistic that Republicans win three to four competitive House seats.

“When you try to pick up more seats, you stretch districts thin, and everything that the Texas Legislature did to improve our congressional seats here in Texas they felt was the right thing to do,” Wilbanks said.

Trump’s Wednesday visit to Texas’s 35th District in San Antonio is one of these redrawn seats. Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R) in Texas’s competitive 15th District, is facing Democrat Johnny Garcia.

“Republicans’ big idea to save their flailing Texas dummymander is to put Donald Trump front and center. There’s just one problem — his approval numbers are in the toilet,” said Madison Andrus, a spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans, on the other hand, maintain the president is the party’s best tool to turnout the base.

“Having President Trump come to Texas is exactly what the Republicans need in the midterms because he is activating our low propensity voters who powered him to a victory in 2024,” one Republican operative said.

One Republican who will not be present at Wednesday night’s rally is Abbott. The governor cited scheduling conflicts, but the move raised eyebrows in Texas and Washington.

“He knows that showing up with the president, and showing up with the president in a big city market like San Antonio is a really bad political idea,” the GOP strategist said.

Others argue that Abbott is likely polling better than public polling suggests, adding that the issue isn’t necessarily whether he will win — rather the margins of his victory.

“He’s probably overperforming the polling a little bit, but it’s a real race for sure,” Steinhauser said.

The senator, who serves as co-chair of the Senate NATO Observer Group, called Republika Srpska a “destabilizing force” during…
articles.body:
Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Wednesday condemned a report that two consultants to President Trump received a large profit from their work advising a pro-Russian government in the Balkans during the U.S. midterm elections cycle.

The senator, who serves as co-chair of the Senate NATO Observer Group, called Republika Srpska a “destabilizing force” during an interview with CNN’s Kasie Hunt.

“These guys are not hurting for money. They don’t need to be doing that,” Tillis said. “They shouldn’t be doing it, and if the reports are true, they should get out of that relationship very, very quickly.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The New York Times reported Tuesday that Chris LaCivita and James Blair traveled to Republica Srpska , a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of the country’s elections Sunday.

The pair, who are leading Trump’s midterm advertising campaign, were reportedly paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each through a Washington-based firm that the country’s government hired to advise on voting issues.

Two people who spoke with the Times noted this work was for the government and not the nationalist party that controls it, but the two are heavily intertwined. Republika Srpska’s dominant party has aligned the country with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Blair previously served as the White House deputy chief of staff before leaving the role in April to run MAGA Inc., the president’s super PAC , during the midterm elections. LaCivita served as a co-manager on Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and is currently a senior adviser to MAGA Inc.

The president appeared to distance himself from the pair Wednesday, calling them “outside consultants,” and said he would terminate them if their work conflicted with the White House.

While Tillis said he would “leave” the decision of whether or not to fire Blair and LaCivita, he urged the advisers to cut ties with the Balkan government.

“This is about knowing your customer, and this customer is bad news for that region and certainly for our partners in the region,” Tillis said, adding, “It’s a horrible look.”

articles.title: Don Lemon says there’s ’65, 70 percent chance’ he runs for president
articles.summary: Former CNN anchor and media personality Don Lemon says he has considered running for president of the U.S. one day, and he put the chances of him doing so at greater than 50 percent. “Look, I never say never. I’ve got a lot on my plate right now doing what I’m doing. This is not…
articles.body:
Former CNN anchor and media personality Don Lemon says he has considered running for president of the U.S. one day, and he put the chances of him doing so at greater than 50 percent.

“Look, I never say never. I’ve got a lot on my plate right now doing what I’m doing. This is not easy to do every day, but I have to be, I am very aware of the importance of what I’m doing, what it means to the culture and society,” Lemon said of his podcast and online commentary show during an appearance on Spencer Macnaughton’s “Uncloseted” podcast.

Lemon started his show after being fired by CNN in 2023.

The pundit called the feedback he gets from people in the community when he is out reporting “very humbling,” and said some of them ask him about pursuing elected office, specifically running for president.

“And I said, ‘Oh, well, definitely. I think I could be a better president than Donald Trump,'” Lemon said. “How serious is it? If the people want me, I’ll do it. But it is a daunting undertaking to run for president in this country because you’d have to be devoted to it full-time. And I would like to devote much of my time to journalism.”

Lemon seemed to suggest it was possible for him to be a candidate for office and a media personality at the same time, saying “maybe that’s a way of running that has not been mined.”

Asked what the chances are he one days announces a bid for the White House, Lemon responded, “What percentage chance that I think I’ll run? … 65, 70.”

“When I’m out there, I’m out there and I cover the candidates and I look at what they do and they’re very good,” he continued. “It makes me wonder my best way of being and operating in this society, whether it is through journalism or if it is through becoming the president of the United States.”

Lemon has been an outspoken critic of President Trump for years. Earlier this year, he was hit with a felony indictment on federal civil rights and conspiracy crimes in connection with his reporting on an anti-Immigrations and Customs Enforcement protest at a Minnesota church.

He has argued Trump’s Justice Department is targeting him because of his views on and criticism of the president.

articles.title: Drugmakers challenge Trump admin pilot program
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story PhRMA sues over drug pricing pilot Drugmakers are challenging a new Trump administration pilot program tying Medicare drug prices to those in other wealthy countries. © AP Photo/John Hanna The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America alleged in the…
articles.body:
Drugmakers are challenging a new Trump administration pilot program tying Medicare drug prices to those in other wealthy countries.

The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America alleged in the lawsuit that the “most favored nation” (MFN) pilot for Medicare, called GLOBE , is unlawful and exceeds the statutory authority of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

PhRMA argued that CMS is using a limited demonstration model authority to impose “nationwide price setting policies that Congress never authorized.”

“The policy doesn’t make medicines more affordable for most beneficiaries, while putting future medical innovation and patient access at risk,” Stephen J. Ubl, president and CEO of PhRMA, said in a statement. “We share the administration’s goal of ensuring Americans can access and afford their medicines, but CMS cannot rewrite the law and bypass Congress to impose foreign price controls.”

The complaint, filed in federal district court in the District of Columbia, asks the court to declare GLOBE unlawful and to vacate the rule in its entirety.

“If allowed to move forward, GLOBE will work immediate and profound harms on American patients and American industry,” the lawsuit states.

Under the rule, drug manufacturers would be required to pay “rebates” to CMS that effectively limit Medicare drug prices to MFN benchmarks based on prices in 19 countries.

The pilot itself isn’t expected to have much of an impact because the administration exempted all but three or four companies in return for their agreement to charge most favored nation prices in Medicaid.

But PhRMA isn’t calling the Medicaid deals “price controls.” The industry group says voluntary agreements are fine, but mandatory participation is not.

PhRMA argues GLOBE is not a test of new or innovative ways to deliver care or pay providers. Instead, they claim CMS is imposing a new pricing requirement that “predetermines the outcome through mandatory manufacturer rebates.”

In the final rule, CMS nodded to the possibility of lawsuits .

“Disagreement with payment policy does not establish a constitutional violation,” the agency wrote.
